# The Weight of Water

Marcus is a 45-year-old military medic who has spent the better part of two decades moving through the world's worst moments with a kind of practiced steadiness. He has triaged soldiers in the field, held pressure on wounds that should not survive, and learned to compartmentalize with the precision his training demanded. He believed, for a long time, that he understood the limits of what a person could endure. Then the floods came.

Three years ago, Marcus was home on extended leave in the small riverside town in southern Germany where he and his wife, Elke, had bought a house with the intention of finally settling down. The flooding that swept through the valley in the early hours of a July morning arrived faster than anyone anticipated. Marcus woke to the sound of Elke calling his name from the hallway. By the time he reached her, the ground floor was already chest-deep in black water. He pushed her toward the staircase, turned back to retrieve his phone and the emergency kit — a reflex so deeply wired it required no thought — and when he turned around again, the current had already taken her. He searched for forty minutes in the dark, in water that was still rising, calling her name until his voice gave out. Elke's body was recovered two days later, a kilometer downstream.

What followed was not grief in any shape Marcus recognized. He returned to duty within six weeks because stillness felt intolerable. He told his commanding officer he was fine. He told himself the same thing with greater conviction. But his body had other ideas.

He cannot sleep for more than two or three hours without waking in a state of absolute certainty that water is rising around him. He lies rigid in the dark, heart hammering, soaked in sweat, and it takes him several minutes to locate himself in time and place. During the day, the intrusions arrive without warning — a running tap, the sound of rain against a window, the particular quality of light on a wet road — and suddenly he is back in that hallway, water at his chest, Elke's voice cutting off mid-sentence. He has learned to read the weather forecast with a vigilance that exhausts him.

At work, his colleagues notice that he has become short-tempered in ways that are unlike him. He snaps at younger medics over procedural errors he would once have corrected patiently. He is hypervigilant in ways that look, from the outside, like professionalism — he is always the first to assess a scene, always positioned near exits, always scanning — but from the inside feel like an alarm that never resets. He is competent. He is also running on something closer to controlled panic than calm.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt that has calcified around the memory of turning away from Elke. He is a medic. He is trained to make triage decisions, to prioritize, to act. He knows, in the part of his mind that can still reason, that turning back for the kit was instinct, not abandonment. But knowledge and belief have become two entirely different countries, and he cannot seem to cross from one to the other. He replays the sequence constantly, adjusting variables — what if he had been faster, what if he had not turned at all — as though the right combination might finally produce a different ending.

He lives alone now in a flat in a city far from any river. He has removed the bathtub and replaced it with a shower. He does not tell people this. He presents to the world as a man who is managing, because managing is what he knows how to do, and because the alternative — admitting that the water is still rising inside him — feels, even now, like a kind of drowning.
